archetype.name: Playoff Team (pass-first offense)
archetype.definition: A team whose top-five passing offense and stout run defense make it the clear AFC South favorite, while a middling pass defense keeps it a tier below the true heavyweights.

report.headline: An offense-first contender whose defense bends more than its points allowed admit.
report.take:
Jacksonville is 4-2, leads a division where nobody else has more than two wins, and has the league's second-best point differential. Last year's 13-4 team leaned on luck, ranking first in wins over expected and first against the spread. This version is built differently. Wins over expected sit at 0.44, close to neutral, and the point differential implies 3.6 wins, so the record is about what the play deserves. The engine has moved from defense to offense: offensive EPA ranks 4th, up from 13th a year ago, while the defense has slid from 5th in EPA allowed to 14th.

The offense runs through Trevor Lawrence's arm. Pass EPA ranks 4th even though the line allows pressure at a below-average rate (21st) and Lawrence holds the ball longer than most (26th in time to throw). He has spread the work across Parker Washington, Brenton Strange and Jakobi Meyers rather than forcing it to one man. The run game is efficient rather than explosive. Bhayshul Tuten carries most of the load, and run EPA ranks 8th even though backs get only 1.8 yards before contact, 30th in the league. The ground game is winning after contact and in short yardage (2nd), not through the blocking up front.

The numbers hide a defense that is better at stopping points than stopping drives. Points allowed ranks 3rd, but yards allowed ranks 20th and EPA allowed 14th. The gap is closed by a 40% red-zone touchdown rate (4th) and a +5 turnover differential. The structure is clear. Run EPA allowed ranks 4th and short-pass EPA allowed ranks 1st, so offenses pass against Jacksonville more than almost anyone (2nd in pass rate over norm). Then they win deep, where the Jaguars rank 29th. Cincinnati threw for 428 yards, and Houston hung 34 after safety Antonio Johnson left at halftime.

The road ahead is shaped by one injury and one schedule quirk. Right tackle Anton Harrison, a 92%-snap starter, tore his ACL during the bye. That hits a line that was already the shakiest part of the offense. The good news is the division: four games remain against Tennessee, Houston and Indianapolis, all with losing records. The bad news is a road-heavy back half that includes Baltimore, Chicago and Dallas away.

strengths.title: Lawrence-led passing game among the league's best
strengths.body: Pass EPA ranks 4th, and the passing game was climbing into the bye, with 300-plus yards in each of the last two games. It produces despite below-average protection, which suggests the efficiency comes from the quarterback and the spread of targets rather than clean pockets. That makes it fairly durable, though losing Harrison will test how much pressure it can absorb.

strengths.title: Run defense that closes the ground
strengths.body: Rush EPA allowed ranks 4th and explosive runs allowed rank 3rd, and several opponents were held to under 25 rushing yards. Offenses respond by abandoning the run, which is why Jacksonville faces one of the strongest pass funnels in the league. This is a stable trait and pays off most against run-reliant offenses.

strengths.title: Winning the turnover and short-yardage margins
strengths.body: A +5 turnover differential (0.8 a game, 5th) and an 88% short-yardage conversion rate (2nd) have kept drives alive on offense and shortened fields for the opponent's offense to cover. Last year's team also ranked near the top in turnover margin, so some of this is real ball security from Lawrence. Expect the takeaway side to be less reliable than the giveaway side.

concerns.title: Deep pass defense is a real hole
concerns.body: Short-pass EPA allowed ranks 1st, but deep EPA allowed ranks 29th, and opposing WR1s average 0.61 EPA per target (29th). The defense is built to take away the underneath game, and teams have learned to throw over it. That is a structural flaw, not noise, and it gets worse if safety Antonio Johnson (86% of snaps, questionable) misses time.

concerns.title: Points allowed flatter than the play
concerns.body: A defense 20th in yards allowed and 14th in EPA allowed is giving up only 17.3 points a game. That rests on a 40% red-zone touchdown rate and on early games against weak offenses. Red-zone rates tend to drift toward average, and the Houston loss looked like what a regression game will look like.

concerns.title: Losing Harrison exposes a thin line
concerns.body: The line was already 21st in pressure rate allowed and 30th in yards before contact, and it commits penalties at a 24th-ranked rate. Now it loses a starting tackle for the season. Penalties have already stalled the offense in spots, with 125 penalty yards at Cincinnati and 100 against Philadelphia. Expect more pressure on Lawrence and a tougher time for Tuten.

trend.note: Results have held near a two-thirds win rate, but the two halves are moving apart. The passing game has gotten steadily more productive since the Week 2 dud in Denver, while the defense allowed its worst passing day at Cincinnati and its most points to Houston.

nextGame.headline: Colts' broken passing game meets a defense built to force it
nextGame.body:
Indianapolis comes in 2-5 with the 27th-ranked offense. Its only real weapon is a run game 4th in rush EPA, and that runs straight into Jacksonville's 4th-ranked run defense, a unit that funnels opponents into passing. Asking Daniel Jones and a passing offense 30th in EPA to throw all day is the matchup Jacksonville wants. On the other side, the Colts generate almost no pressure (31st), which softens the blow of Harrison's absence. Jacksonville is coming off a bye at home, and the Book has it at -7.5 with a 46.5 total. The forecast more than five days out shows a chance of thunderstorms, worth watching but not worth building on.

Availability tilts toward Jacksonville. The Colts are without tight end Tyler Warren and cornerback Sauce Gardner, both near-every-snap starters. Corner Justin Walley is questionable, and deep threat Alec Pierce stays on IR, which takes some sting out of Jacksonville's deep-ball problem. For the Jaguars, Harrison is out for the year, and the swing piece is safety Antonio Johnson, questionable with the ankle that knocked him out of the Houston game.

waysToWin.title: Lawrence carves a depleted, pressure-less secondary
waysToWin.body: The Colts rank 31st in pressure rate and are missing Gardner, so Lawrence should have time even with a patched right tackle. Their defense has also been soft on third receivers and tight ends, which suits a passing game that spreads targets to Meyers and Strange. This is the most direct path to an early lead.

waysToWin.title: Take away the run, make Jones throw
waysToWin.body: Indianapolis's offense works only on the ground, with rush EPA 4th and pass EPA 30th. Jacksonville's run defense is 4th in rush EPA allowed and forces opponents to pass. If the Colts fall behind and have to drop back, a line with a 23rd-ranked sack rate meets a Jaguars front that pressures at the 8th-best rate.

waysToWin.title: Win the turnover battle again
waysToWin.body: The Colts sit last in turnover differential per game and have only 3 takeaways all season. Jacksonville protects the ball and has taken it away in most games. One or two short fields would likely put the game out of reach.

waysToLose.title: Getting beaten over the top
waysToLose.body: Jacksonville's deep defense ranks 29th, and if Johnson can't go, the back end is thinner still. Even a weak passing offense can steal a game with two or three completions downfield. That is how Houston and Cincinnati moved the ball.

waysToLose.title: A slow, close game on Indy's terms
waysToLose.body: The Colts are 5th in time of possession and 4th on third-down defense, so they can shrink the game and keep it within a score. Jacksonville already struggled to separate from a bad Philadelphia team as a 7.5-point favorite. If the run defense slips, this becomes a coin flip late.

waysToLose.title: Flags and a reshuffled line
waysToLose.body: Jacksonville's line penalties already rank 24th, and a new tackle tends to draw holding calls and false starts. The Colts are the least-penalized team in the league, so they won't hand back yardage. Drives killed by penalties are the easiest way for Jacksonville to waste its talent edge.

nextGame.watch: How the right side of the line holds up without Harrison in the first quarter: whether Lawrence gets clean pockets against a pass rush that rarely gets home.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense looks sustainable, because passing efficiency carries over from week to week better than almost anything else. The run game's after-contact production should hold even if the Harrison loss trims it. The defense is where to expect regression. Its red-zone stinginess and points allowed have outrun its yardage and EPA numbers, and the deep-ball weakness hasn't been fixed. Points allowed should drift up toward the low 20s.

The schedule is a mix. Four of the last ten are division games against teams with losing records, which makes the AFC South Jacksonville's to lose. But road trips to Baltimore, Chicago, Dallas and the Giants, plus Pittsburgh's 6th-ranked defense at home, will test a pass defense and a patched line. A double-digit win total and a division title are the likeliest outcome. A top seed depends on the defense finding a fix for deep balls.
swingFactors: Pass protection after Harrison's ACL tear
Whether the deep pass defense tightens, with Antonio Johnson healthy
How much the red-zone and takeaway luck regresses

confidence.note: Six games, a key line injury, and a defense whose points outrun its underlying numbers.
